records.our_prose: Pear trees flower in early spring, usually a little earlier than apples, which means a late frost is more likely to catch the open blossoms. Different varieties bloom a few days apart, spread over about two weeks, and two trees can only pollinate each other if they bloom at the same time. Pear flowers are not a bee favorite, so warm, calm weather during bloom really helps the bees do their work and set a good crop.

records.our_prose: A long-lived deciduous fruit tree (Pyrus communis) grown for fresh-eating, dessert, and storage fruit. European pear is a cross-pollination crop: most cultivars are self-unfruitful, so you plant two different varieties whose bloom periods overlap and rely on bees to move pollen between them (a few, like Bartlett and Anjou, are partially self-fruitful in mild climates but still crop better with a pollinizer). The signature difference from apple is at harvest: European pears ripen OFF the tree. Pick them mature but firm and green, give them a cool rest, then ripen at room temperature; a pear left to ripen on the branch goes mealy and rotten at the core. Fire blight is the major disease, worst in warm, humid regions, so cultivar and rootstock resistance matter. Chill requirement is variety-set, and rootstock choice sets mature size and how soon the tree bears.

records.our_prose: This is the most important thing about growing pears: one pear tree alone usually will not make fruit. Pear flowers need pollen from a DIFFERENT pear variety, carried by bees. So plan to plant two different kinds of European pear, not two of the same, within about 50 to 100 ft of each other, and make sure they bloom at the same time. A couple of varieties (Bartlett, Anjou) can set a small crop on their own in mild areas, but even they do much better with a partner. Watch out for one famous mismatch: Bartlett and Seckel cannot pollinate each other, so give each of them a different partner like Bosc or Comice. And a few varieties (like Magness) cannot pollinate anything and need two partners themselves, so ask the nursery before you rely on one as your second tree.

records.our_prose: If your tree comes bare-root (bare roots, no pot), plant it in late winter or early spring while it is still leafless and dormant, as soon as you can dig the soil. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough that the roots spread out without folding. The key thing: find the graft union (the bumpy spot low on the trunk where the top variety was joined to the roots) and keep it about 2 to 3 in above the soil, never bury it. Fill the hole with the same soil you dug out, water well, and tie small trees to a stake. A potted tree is planted the same way and can go in anytime through spring.

records.source_context: Mainly, you want to prune a tree to have well-spaced branches and a balanced appearance, while eliminating problem branches (those that are broken, diseased or dead). Fruit trees should be pruned every year in late winter or early spring, after the coldest weather is past and before growth begins. Prune minimally, especially with young trees, as excessive pruning will delay or reduce fruiting and create too much leafy growth.

records.our_prose: Plant a bare-root tree while fully dormant, late winter to early spring, as soon as the ground is workable. Soak the roots in water for an hour or two before planting, dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending, and set the tree so the graft union (the swollen knob where the variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 in above the final soil line, burying it lets the variety root over and defeats the rootstock. Backfill with native soil, water in to settle, and stake dwarf and quince stocks. A potted tree follows the same depth rule but can go in through spring.
